newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - March 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - March 31.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- MORGAN ANALYST SENT HOME OVER SOLV-EX INVOLVEMENT

Senior oil analyst at Morgan Grenfell in New York, Charles Maxwell, has been sent on "gardening leave" following his admission that he sent an informal memorandum to institutional bosses with recommendations that they should follow Solv-EX, an extraction company based in New Mexico.
-- RECOVERY SEES MORE FIRMS HIT CASH PROBLEMS

According to Trade Indemnity, Britain's leading credit insurance group, business failures and bad debts are rising again despite the economic recovery. Trade Indemnity had recorded an annual fall in the rate of failures and bad debts for every quarter since 1992, but last year the trend reversed and by the final three months the annual rate was 14 percent worse than a year earlier.
-- THAMES IN TALKS TO SUPPLY JAKARTA

Thames Water Plc is in talks to sign a 245 million stg contract to manage the water supply for half of Jakarta. A spokesman for Thames Water said that the company is in deep negotiations with the Indonesian government that a deal is expected to be signed within the next few weeks. It would be Thames' biggest foreign water contract to date.
THE TIMES
-- BROWN WARNED AGAINST CUTS TO TAX BREAKS FOR PENSIONS

Actuaries have estimated that plans being considered by shadow chancellor, Gordon Brown, to hit the tax privileges of Britain's 650 billion stg pension funds could backfire, costing as much as 9 billion stg in lost tax revenue. It is estimated that the move could cost the Treasury more in corporation tax than it saved and that half of the UK's company pension schemes could be pushed into deficit by Labour's plans.
-- SEARS SALES A STEP BEHIND SHOE SECTOR

Sears subsidiary, and owner of Dolcis, Shoe City and Cable & Co, British Shoe Corporation is lagging behind the rest of the footwear industry in the first quarter of this year according to industry experts. It is claimed that BSC has shown no sales growth compared with a four percent industry rise and with Stead & Simpson showing a rise of nine percent.
THE GUARDIAN
-- GAS GROUP SEEKS POVERTY QUOTA

The Gas Consumers Council said domestic gas supply companies should be made to take on a set percentage of low-income customers to stop firms cherry-picking better off households. An alternative proposal is to limit the range of tariffs charged to different types of customer, reducing the premium on pre-payment meters, mainly used by low-income customers.
-- SECOND MUTUAL IN AMP'S SIGHTS

There is mounting speculation that Australian Mutual Provident is set to bid for National Provident Institution, one of Britain's oldest pensions companies, following last week's defeat in the auction for Scottish Amicable. Insurance industry experts expect AMP to make an offer for NPI which could trigger big pay outs for its 390,000 members.
-- PROPERTY RIVALS BATTLE IT OUT

The MEPC property company was forced to defend its position on Sunday night following news of a take-over approach from its smaller rival Hammerson. The two groups have been in merger talks which if advanced would create a group worth 3.2 billion stg. MEPC was believed to be angry that news of the six week talks was leaked and claims that Hammerson has not yet put forward detailed proposals.
THE INDEPENDENT
No business section today due to public holiday.
